modules.title: The perceptron
modules.summary: The single-unit linear classifier the rest of the course builds on: one weighted sum, one threshold, one straight decision boundary.
objectives: State the perceptron's decision rule and compute its output for a given input.
Update a perceptron's weights by hand using the perceptron learning rule.
Explain why a single perceptron cannot separate a non-linearly-separable dataset like XOR.

difficulty.rationale: The perceptron is the right place to start: one linear boundary, one weight update, and the geometry is visible in two dimensions. Nothing here requires calculus or vectorized notation yet, and everything the cohort has asked about so far is the decision rule's limits, not the mechanics of computing it.
evidence: Every student replicated the OR and AND decision boundaries correctly on the first pass through the material.
The XOR question in #questions is the only place a limit of the single perceptron has come up — no one has struggled with the update rule itself.

modules.title: Multilayer perceptrons
modules.summary: Stacking perceptron-like units with a nonlinearity between layers, so the network can represent boundaries a single line never could.
objectives: Describe why stacking linear layers without a nonlinearity collapses to a single linear layer.
Compute a forward pass through a two-layer MLP by hand, then in matrix form.
Justify a choice of hidden layer width and depth for a small classification problem.

difficulty.rationale: Multilayer perceptrons are where the course moves from one line to a function built from several lines composed with a nonlinearity between them — that composition, not the arithmetic, is what the cohort trips on. The forward-pass formula is easy to copy; trusting what each hidden unit is actually computing is not.
evidence: Assignment 1 needed the scalar forward pass spelled out before the matrix form — Ignacio's report showed the matrix formula was correct with no sense of what a hidden unit was doing.
Two of three students could write `Z = X @ W + b` but not state the shape of `Z` without checking.

modules.title: Backpropagation
modules.summary: The chain rule applied layer by layer to a network, to find how much each weight is responsible for the final error.
objectives: Derive the gradient of the loss with respect to a weight using the chain rule.
Explain why the derivative of the activation — not the activation itself — appears in the backward pass.
Identify when gradients vanish or explode across layers and why.

difficulty.rationale: Backpropagation itself is mechanical once the chain rule is set up correctly, but that setup is exactly where the cohort is slipping: multiplying by the activation instead of its derivative erases the one place the network can tell how the error should split across a hidden layer.
evidence: 2 of 3 students multiplied by σ(z) instead of σ′(z) in Assignment 2.
Assignment 1 showed partial derivatives are fresh, so the chain rule needed to restate them rather than assume them.

modules.title: Attention
modules.summary: Where the course goes after backprop: attention as a weighted lookup, and why it replaced recurrence.
objectives: Compute scaled dot-product attention by hand on a 3-token example
Explain what the softmax over scores buys over a plain average
Say in one sentence why attention parallelizes where recurrence cannot

messages.text: Assignment 2 feedback is out. Ada wrote each of you a note on how it went — open My study to read it.
Thanks Ada, the note was clear — already rereading the chain-rule card.
Why can't a single perceptron learn XOR? I can get it to learn AND and OR fine, but XOR just won't converge no matter how long I train it.

A single perceptron can only draw one straight decision boundary through the input space, so it can only solve problems where one line (or hyperplane) separates the two classes. AND and OR are both linearly separable — one line puts every positive example on one side — so the perceptron converges on both. [[modules/01-perceptron/linear-separability.md|Linear separability and XOR]] walks through why.

XOR isn't linearly separable: no single straight line separates its positive and negative examples, no matter how the weights are trained. That's not a training problem — it's a limit on what one linear boundary can represent, and it's exactly why a lone perceptron can't solve it. Stacking perceptrons with a nonlinearity between them, which is the next module, is what fixes it.
That's the one, thanks — makes sense now.
